notes: Maritime service-out and forum conveniens judgment; CPR 6.20 damage construction and Fatal Accidents Act dependency are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Service out and forum for ship engineer death claim

statutes_considered.title: Rome Convention on the law applicable to contractual obligations

key_facts: Clifford Booth, chief engineer on the MV MAYSORA, died in Egypt when a defective livestock loading ramp collapsed during repair work.
His widow sued the master in England and sought permission to serve the ship owners and managers out of the jurisdiction.
The master applied for a stay on forum non conveniens grounds, arguing Jordan was the more appropriate forum.
Defendants had instructed counsel to take every available technical point on jurisdiction to dissuade the widow from pursuing the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to stay proceedings against the master and to set aside permission for service out of the jurisdiction on the other defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; permission to serve out upheld on necessary-or-proper-party and damage-in-jurisdiction grounds; England held the proper forum for trial.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 6.20(8)(a), 'damage' means harm sustained by the claimant and is not limited to the damage completing the tort, so dependency and funeral expenses sustained in England can ground jurisdiction where death occurred abroad; where all defendants can be sued together in England and Jordan offers no reliable alternative, England is the forum conveniens.
legal_issues: Whether there was a real issue between the claimant and the master justifying service out on a necessary or proper party basis
Whether the employment contract was governed by English law under the Rome Convention
Whether dependency and funeral expenses constituted damage sustained within the jurisdiction under CPR 6.20(8)(a)
Whether Jordan was clearly or distinctly the more appropriate forum

notes: Tomlin Order commercial settlement enforcement; Union Eagle and specific performance points are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Tomlin Order breach: no equity relief on share settlement
key_facts: A Tomlin Order settled long-running litigation over shares in Crampton Bros (Coopers) Limited following Ada Crampton's death.
Mr Hurst agreed to pay £190,000 in costs and to purchase 100 gift shares, with time of the essence for a £40,000 payment by 18 March 2004.
If Mr Hurst breached those conditions, he would lose the right to buy 100 shares and Harold Crampton Junior would receive all 400 gift shares.
Lloyd J found Mr Hurst in breach on three grounds and ordered specific performance of paragraph 8(3) of the Tomlin Order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal and a stay of Lloyd J's construction and enforcement of a Tomlin Order.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no permission to appeal or stay granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where a commercial settlement makes time of the essence and sets out clear consequences for breach, equity will not relieve against forfeiture or treat the bargain as penal; a party who undertakes to procure third-party cooperation may be ordered to perform specifically unless circumstances have materially changed.
legal_issues: Whether equity should relieve against forfeiture for late payment under a Tomlin Order
Whether the settlement terms were penal
Whether the judge was wrong to order specific performance of an obligation to procure third parties
Whether the application should be adjourned for representation
linked_authorities: Union Eagle Ltd v Golden Achievement Ltd [1997] AC 514

confidence.notes: Core equitable and contractual principles and outcome are clear. Detailed family litigation history is background only.

notes: School abuse insurance preliminary issue; affirmation and Third Parties Act analysis is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: School abuse claim: insurer avoidance and affirmation
key_facts: Graham Spriggs is the lead claimant in group litigation alleging sexual and physical abuse at Wessington Court School between 1965 and 1983.
The dissolved school company was restored to the register so claims could proceed against its public liability insurers, RSA as successor to Phoenix Assurance.
RSA conceded it could avoid policies for non-disclosure by headmaster Dennis Eagles but disputed affirmation and cover before 17 May 1973.
Claimants relied on Berrymans' September 2002 letter stating RSA 'are on risk' and conduct at a case management conference as affirmation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue on whether RSA was obliged to indemnify the school and over what period.
enrichment.outcome: RSA entitled to avoid the Phoenix public liability policies; claimants failed to prove Phoenix cover before 17 May 1973 and failed to establish affirmation.
enrichment.ratio: Affirmation of an insurance contract must be communicated to the insured, not merely to a third-party claimant under the 1930 Act; statements that an insurer is 'on risk' in correspondence about existence and terms of cover do not amount to an unequivocal election to affirm where liability and avoidance remain in dispute.
legal_issues: Whether Phoenix insured the school before 17 May 1973
Whether RSA affirmed the policies before serving a defence purporting to avoid them
Whether communication to the claimant rather than the insured could constitute affirmation
Whether Berrymans' letter and Mr Nash's CMC conduct were unequivocal affirmations with requisite knowledge

notes: Estate administration costs appeal; dual charging and FACS-adjacent costs principles are clear though quantification is reserved.

enrichment.short_title: Estate solicitors' dual time and value charge upheld
key_facts: KBL solicitors charged £592,983.40 for administering Sir Geoffrey Hulton's estate, including a 1.5% value charge and time charges.
The Court of Appeal held solicitors may charge separately for value as well as time, subject to fair and reasonable overall remuneration.
Costs Judge Rogers assessed total remuneration at £500,000, including a value element of £141,906.71.
Jemma Trust, as residuary beneficiary's assignee, appealed three assessment decisions on value charge, procedural fairness, and attendance notes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with assessors against three decisions in a detailed assessment of solicitors' estate administration bills.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all three grounds.
enrichment.ratio: In assessing a separate value charge under the 1994 Remuneration Order, a costs judge may have regard to all relevant factors in arriving at a globally fair and reasonable figure, provided he remains conscious of what has already been reflected in the time charge; absence of attendance notes does not automatically disallow time where the judge is satisfied the time was reasonably spent.
legal_issues: Whether the costs judge wrongly took non-value factors into account when assessing the value charge
Whether failure to apply the Court of Appeal's regressive scale invalidated the assessment
Whether procedural unfairness arose from cross-examination without witness statements on individual bill items
Whether time should be reduced for inadequate attendance notes

notes: Planning enforcement fall-back appeal; five grounds analysed in detail with statutory interpretation obiter on s.174 and s.173.

enrichment.short_title: Boat storage enforcement: fall-back permission weight
key_facts: East Devon Council granted planning permission in 2001 for boat storage racks at Exmouth Marina, but the appellants erected taller differently positioned racks without compliance.
An enforcement notice was served and appealed; a first inspector dismissed the appeal partly over whether top-tier boat storage was permitted.
Sullivan J remitted the appeal after holding the 2001 permission did not prohibit storage on top of the permitted structures.
A second inspector dismissed the remitted appeal, giving little weight to the 2001 permission as a fall-back because implementation seemed theoretical.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 289 against a remitted enforcement notice decision of the Secretary of State.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all five grounds; enforcement appeal decision upheld though the judge identified errors of law on statutory interpretation that did not affect the result.
enrichment.ratio: On remittal after a successful section 289 appeal, the inspector may reconsider the whole enforcement appeal afresh and is not bound by issue estoppel from the earlier written-representations stage; the likelihood of a fall-back permission being implemented is a material planning judgment to which little weight may be given if prospects are more theoretical than real.
legal_issues: Whether issue estoppel prevented the second inspector from reassessing the fall-back position
Whether the inspector erred in assessing the likelihood of implementing the 2001 permission
Whether the modified scheme was wrongly compared with the unauthorised rather than permitted development
Whether the inspector misapplied the fall-back test from Ahern and South Buckinghamshire
Whether planning permission on a ground (a) appeal may authorise materially different retained structures and whether conditions may be imposed after a ground (f) under-enforcement

notes: Waste prosecution JR refused as premature; Article 7 and abuse-of-process analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Waste prosecution: premature Article 7 judicial review
key_facts: Paul Rackham Ltd was prosecuted for treating, keeping and depositing controlled waste at Camp Farm in 1999 and 2000.
The company argued Material A and Product A were recovered products, not waste, and that ARCO Chemie changed the law retrospectively.
District Judge Healy refused a stay for abuse of process and declined to state a case; the company sought permission for judicial review.
The Environment Agency's decision to prosecute and alleged failures in testing and exemption registration were also challenged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review of magistrates' court refusal to stay waste prosecution proceedings and to state a case.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; prosecution to proceed in the magistrates' court.
enrichment.ratio: Challenges based on Article 7 ECHR uncertainty in the definition of waste and alleged abuse in the decision to prosecute require a factual matrix best resolved at trial rather than by premature judicial review; ARCO Chemie did not create retrospective criminal liability but developed case-by-case interpretation of when waste ceases to be waste.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution for 1999 conduct infringed Article 7 after ARCO Chemie
Whether the waste definition was too uncertain to satisfy Article 7
Whether the Environment Agency's decision to prosecute was an abuse of process
Whether the magistrates' court had jurisdiction to entertain the Article 7 stay application
Whether non-registration of a Schedule 3 exemption defeated the prosecution

notes: FACS community care challenge; eligibility framework error identified but overall care plan not quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Community care hours for disabled Still's disease claimant

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Mr Heffernan is severely disabled by Still's Disease and almost total blindness and receives community care from Sheffield City Council.
After complaints and panel review, his care was increased to 24.5 hours per week including 7.5 hours from Supporting People funding.
He challenged the February 2004 assessment under Fair Access to Care Services guidance as flawed and irrational.
The council's eligibility criteria wrongly placed 'health problems' in bands below 'critical', contrary to FACS paragraph 16.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of community care assessment and care plan following amended grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; care plan not held perverse but local authority must reconsider assessment in light of identified FACS errors.
enrichment.ratio: Under FACS, presenting needs must be fully assessed and risks allocated to eligibility bands using the prescribed wording; significant health problems belong only in the critical band, but a procedural error in eligibility criteria does not automatically make a particular hours allocation irrational without fresh assessment.
legal_issues: Whether the council properly applied FACS presenting and eligible needs guidance
Whether the eligibility criteria unlawfully replicated health problems across non-critical bands
Whether 24.5 hours care was irrational given flare-ups and emergencies
Whether medical appointment support was wrongly excluded from social care provision

confidence.notes: FACS legal error is clearly identified but relief was limited to reconsideration rather than quashing. Factual care needs assessment was not disputed.

notes: CPS reversal prosecution stay; Bloomfield abuse-of-process principles applied on case stated appeal.

enrichment.short_title: CPS reversal of no-prosecution decision stayed as abuse
key_facts: Mr Taylor drove a bus onto an A1 slip road where a car indicating left continued straight on at about 30 mph, causing a fatal collision.
Three CPS lawyers initially decided there was insufficient evidence for careless driving, then reversed that decision after family representations.
Mr Taylor was told on 12 June 2003 that no action would be taken, then notified on 18 July 2003 that prosecution would proceed.
Alnwick magistrates stayed the information as vexatious or an abuse of process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' decision to stay careless driving proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Where the CPS gives an unqualified assurance that no prosecution will follow, a later change of mind may be an abuse unless the original decision was clearly wrong on the evidential test alone; a rational public-interest decision not to prosecute after a genuine mistake can support reliance on the assurance even without severe prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether the original CPS decision not to prosecute was clearly wrong
Whether the CPS decision was based solely on the evidential test or also on public interest
Whether reversing the decision after an assurance amounted to a vexatious or abusive prosecution
Whether Bloomfield principles applied
linked_authorities: R v Bloomfield 1 Cr App R 135

confidence.notes: Abuse-of-process reasoning is clear though the original CPS decision-making process was not fully evidenced.

notes: Equitable subrogation to unsecured debt after forged mortgage; Banque Financiere and Boscawen analysis is extensive.

enrichment.short_title: Subrogation to unsecured debt after forged mortgage
key_facts: Mr Filby forged his wife's signature on a remortgage of 52 Gainsborough with Mortgage Express in May 1990.
£40,859 discharged the Halifax mortgage and £60,801 was paid to reduce a joint Midland Bank development loan account.
Mrs Filby was not estopped from denying the mortgage; the lender was subrogated to the Halifax charge.
The lender also claimed subrogation to Midland Bank's unsecured personal rights over the joint loan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against county court order granting equitable subrogation to unsecured Midland Bank loan rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claimants entitled to subrogation to Midland Bank's unsecured personal rights to the extent of £60,801.
enrichment.ratio: Where advance money was paid under a void mortgage contract and used to reduce a joint unsecured debt, the lender retained beneficial ownership until payment and may be subrogated to the creditor's personal rights despite absence of security, provided the enrichment was at the lender's expense and the lender did not receive the bargained-for security.
legal_issues: Whether the lender retained a proprietary interest in remortgage funds after discharging the Halifax mortgage
Whether payment to Midland Bank was at the lender's or Mr Filby's expense
Whether subrogation can attach to unsecured as well as secured debts
Whether solicitors' breach of trust terms preserved the lender's beneficial interest

notes: Patent licence stay refused; English jurisdiction clause in multinational licence is central.

enrichment.short_title: Patent licence stay refused despite US proceedings
key_facts: Celltech licensed MedImmune under Adair patent rights worldwide, with English law and exclusive English court jurisdiction for contract disputes.
MedImmune sells SYNAGIS and disputes royalty liability under US Adair 2; it commenced US invalidity and non-infringement proceedings.
Celltech began English proceedings and applied for a streamlined procedure; MedImmune sought a stay pending the US action.
Earlier English actions on other Adair patents had failed on US file wrapper estoppel and German infringement grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to stay English patent infringement proceedings and to order a streamlined Patents Court procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Stay refused; parties held to the jurisdiction clause; streamlined procedure ordered in principle subject to agreed directions.
enrichment.ratio: A non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause in a multinational patent licence binds the parties to litigate infringement disputes in England unless strong reasons exist; parallel US proceedings and possible squeeze arguments are ordinary factors already contemplated by such clauses and do not justify overriding the agreed forum.
legal_issues: Whether parallel US proceedings were a strong reason to stay English infringement proceedings
Whether clause 13 covered disputes over whether SYNAGIS fell within US Adair 2 claims
Whether 'performance' under the licence meant payment mechanics only or included infringement scope
Whether a streamlined procedure was appropriate
